subsection: 5. Voluntary and statutory consumer protection bodies

notes.b: Consumer protection bodies are either established by law with legal powers, or operate voluntarily through advice, research and self-regulation.
points: Statutory bodies are established by an Act of the Oireachtas and have legal powers to investigate, enforce and, in some cases, prosecute.
Voluntary bodies are independent or industry-based; they advise, research, lobby and handle complaints, but they cannot compel a trader to act.
Self-regulation: the advertising industry sets its own standards through a code, and a voluntary body handles public complaints under that code.
A consumer with a complaint about a trader should usually approach the trader first, then a statutory or voluntary body.

notes.b: The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission is the state body that enforces consumer law.
points: Enforces the Consumer Protection Act 2007 and other consumer law.
Investigates unfair and illegal trading practices, including false or misleading advertising and pricing.
Can prosecute offences under consumer law.
Informs consumers of their rights through its website and helpline, and runs consumer information campaigns.
Enforces non-food product safety rules.
Advises government on consumer issues.

notes.h: Citizens Information and the Citizens Information Board (statutory)
notes.b: Citizens Information provides free, confidential information and advice on rights and entitlements.
points: The Citizens Information Board is a statutory body that funds and oversees Citizens Information services.
Citizens Information Centres are local, independent services that give free, confidential information on consumer issues.
Services cover consumer issues, social welfare entitlements, housing and other rights.
The Citizens Information website and phone service give access to information on rights from anywhere in Ireland.

notes.h: Office of the Ombudsman and Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (statutory)
notes.b: Ombudsman offices investigate complaints that have not been resolved directly with the body concerned.
points: The Office of the Ombudsman investigates complaints about the administrative actions of public bodies, such as government departments and the HSE.
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman investigates complaints about financial service providers, such as banks, insurers and pension providers.
Both are a last resort: the consumer must first use the provider's or body's own complaints procedure.
Investigations are free of charge to the complainant.

notes.b: The FSAI protects consumers from food-related risks.
points: Established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998.
Sets food safety standards, monitors food safety and gives consumer advice on food.
Works with official control agencies, such as the HSE and local authorities, that inspect food businesses.

notes.b: The Consumers' Association of Ireland is an independent organisation that represents consumers.
points: Researches and tests goods and services and publishes its findings in Consumer Choice.
Provides objective information and advice on consumer products and services, including a personal advisory service.
Lobbies government on consumer issues and represents consumers on a number of bodies.

notes.b: The Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland is a self-regulatory body for advertising.
points: Promotes high standards in advertising, requiring that marketing communications are legal, decent, honest and truthful.
Investigates complaints from the public about advertisements, such as false claims or offensive content.
Can recommend that an advertisement be altered, or require that it be withdrawn.
Trade associations look after the interests of their members and may have codes of practice and complaints procedures.
European Consumer Centre Ireland gives advice on buying goods or services from traders in other EU countries.

keyTerms.definition: A body established by law with legal powers to investigate, enforce and in some cases prosecute.
An independent or industry-based body that advises, researches and lobbies, without legal power to compel a trader.
The practice by which an industry sets and polices its own standards, often through a code.
Putting the case for consumers to government so that policy and law reflect consumer interests.
Bringing a criminal case against a trader for an offence under consumer law.
An organisation of businesses in one sector that protects its members' interests and sets their standards.
Written rules of conduct that an industry or association agrees to follow.
The final step in a complaints process, reached only after the trader or provider has been given a chance to resolve the matter.

factCards.term: Three functions of the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
factCards.definition: Enforces consumer law and investigates unfair or illegal trading practices; informs consumers of their rights; advises government on consumer issues.
Free, confidential information on rights and entitlements, and advice on consumer issues.

factCards.term: Role of the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
factCards.definition: Investigates complaints about financial service providers, as a last resort after the provider's own complaints process.

factCards.term: Two functions of the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland
factCards.definition: Promotes legal, decent, honest and truthful advertising; investigates public complaints and can require advertisements to be changed or withdrawn.

factCards.term: Three activities of the Consumers' Association of Ireland
factCards.definition: Researches goods and services and publishes findings; provides objective information and advice; lobbies government on consumer issues.

factCards.term: Main difference between legally established and advisory consumer organisations
factCards.definition: Legally established bodies have statutory powers to investigate and enforce; advisory bodies rely on research, advice and self-regulation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a statutory body and a voluntary body concerned with consumer protection, naming one of each.
questions.model: Statutory body: set up by law, with legal powers to investigate, enforce and prosecute; for example the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission. Voluntary body: independent or industry-based, offering advice, research, lobbying and complaint handling, but with no power to compel a trader to act; for example the Consumers' Association of Ireland or the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland. Other correct names are acceptable, provided the distinction in legal powers is made.

questions.prompt: Discuss the role of at least three bodies, statutory and voluntary, that help a consumer who has a complaint about an advertisement or a faulty service.
questions.model: Advertisement: the Advertising Standards Authority of Ireland, a voluntary self-regulatory body, investigates public complaints about false, misleading or offensive advertising and can require changes or withdrawal of the advertisement. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, a statutory body, investigates misleading advertising and pricing and can prosecute offences under the Consumer Protection Act 2007. Faulty service or goods: Citizens Information, a statutory service through the Citizens Information Board, gives free, confidential advice on rights and how to complain. The Consumers' Association of Ireland, a voluntary body, gives objective advice and represents consumers. For a complaint against a financial service provider, the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman investigates as a last resort. A complete answer distinguishes the legal powers of statutory bodies from the advice and self-regulation offered by voluntary bodies.
